study.title: Jeremiah 29 - Letter to the exiles, true hope and judgment on lies
study.overview: Jeremiah 29 records a letter sent to the Jews already taken to Babylon. Instead of feeding the illusion of an immediate return, the prophet, speaking in the name of the LORD, guides the exiles to settle on the discipline of captivity: build, plant, form families, seek the good of the city where they live and pray for it. At the same time, God denounces the false prophets who promised quick deliverance without being sent. The center of the message is that captivity will have a certain time - seventy years, but it will not be the end of the covenant: there will be divine visitation, restoration and return. The chapter ends with the condemnation of Shemaiah, who tried to silence Jeremiah and keep the people attached to the lie.

outline.title: Letter to the exiles: to accept discipline and seek the Lord
outline.explanation: Jeremiah writes to the captives in Babylon, and in the name of the LORD of hosts he sends them to live in a stable way in exile: they build houses, plant themselves, marry, have children, and seek the peace of the city to which they were taken. Instruction is not a resignation without hope, but obedient submission to the time of God. The prophet also corrects confidence in the dreams and messages of false prophets. The LORD defines the limit of exile: seventy years, after which there will be visitation, restoration and return. Verses 12-14 highlight that the restoration goes through prayer and sincere search of God with all your heart.

outline.title: The lie of the prophets and the fate of those who rejected the word
outline.explanation: The people who stayed in Jerusalem assumed to have an advantage over the exiles, as if God had raised up prophets only in Babylon. The LORD answers that also those who have remained in Jerusalem will come sword, famine, and pestilence, because they have not heard their words. He then names Ahab and Zedekiah, liar prophets who spoke in his name without permission. The judgment on them would be public and shameful, and their death would become an example and curse among the exiles. The text reinforces that speaking falsely in the name of God is not a light error, but rebellion against the Lord himself.

outline.title: Semaiah, the Opposition Letter and the Final Judgment
outline.explanation: Shemaiah, the Neelamite, sends another letter trying to frame Jeremiah as a threat and encourage repression against him. He wants the priest Zephaniah and other priests to arrest the prophet, because Jeremiah taught that captivity would be long. The LORD then reveals to Jeremiah that Shemaiah spoke without being sent and made the people trust lies. The sentence is severe: punishment on Shemaiah and his offspring, without permanence among the people and without participation in the good that God would do to his people. The rebellion here is not only against a prophet, but against the LORD who sent him.

study.context: The chapter is located at the time when part of Judah had already been deported to Babylon after the departure of Jeconiah, Queen Mother, Princes and Specialized Workers. The text itself links the letter to the deportation scenario and mentions an embassy sent by Zedekiah. The given notes indicate that the aforementioned deportation is that of 597 before Christ. The chapter shows a conflict between the true word of God and religious messages that promised rapid liberation.
study.theology: Jeremiah 29 teaches that biblical hope is not a denial of reality, but trust in God's sovereignty over the time of discipline and restoration. The exile was no chance or abandonment; it was God's action, and so the correct answer was to obey, build a possible life and seek peace where it was. The chapter also shows that God rejects religious falsehood: speaking in his name without submission is lies and rebellion. The promise of God in 11-14 is not an amulet for immediate comfort, but a call to the sincere pursuit of the Lord, who hears, lets himself be found and restored. Thus, the hope of the people is not in the prophets that please, but in the God who disciplines and then visits with goodness.

scholarViews.insight: The letter was sent to the exiles in Babylon and should be read repeatedly among the scattered groups, reaching all the people taken captive.
Jeremiah exhorts the captives to conform to the present situation, making the best of it rather than feeding expectations of immediate return.
The seventy years must be fulfilled in full; before that, relief from captivity should not be expected.

questions: In which areas have I confused hope in God in haste by immediate answers?
Have I searched for the good of the city and the people around me, even in difficult circumstances, or just my own way out?
What voices have shaped my trust: the Word of the Lord or messages that promise what I desire to hear?
study.practice: This passage calls the Christian to live faithfully where God placed him, even when the situation is not ideal. Instead of cultivating bitterness or emotional escape, it is wise to establish habits of life, serve the common good and pray for those who rule and for those who live around. It is also necessary to discern religious messages by Scripture, because not every speech in the name of God comes from God. Finally, true restoration begins when the heart turns to the Lord with sincerity, in prayer and repentance.
study.uncertainty: The given notes do not allow to accurately affirm the exact date of the letter beyond the general reference to the period of captivity of 597 before Christ mentioned by Tyndale. There is also the possibility, indicated by commentators, that the chapter meets more than one letter, but this is presented as an interpretative hypothesis, not as an undeniable data of the text. No historical or linguistic details were used other than that in the notes.
